paras: The threatened lynching of Otho Gilmore took place at Martin's Ferry, Belmont County, Ohio, on the night of July 26, 1882, when a large crowd talked of hanging Gilmore, a Black prisoner, after he cut a police officer and a citizen with a razor in the town lockup. A guard was placed at the jail, and the crowd broke up once the wounded men were expected to live. Gilmore, who had been shot twice by the officer, recovered and was sentenced in December to four years in the penitentiary.

Gilmore, described as a 'colored man' of 45 and the father of six children, was arrested on the evening of Tuesday, July 25, for drunkenness and was fined $3 and costs by Mayor Mitchell the next morning. Unable to pay, he was held in the lockup, from which he escaped late on the afternoon of July 26 through a hole in the wall. Officer William Linn (spelled Lynn in some papers) caught him about 8:30 that evening near John Burkhart's store and brought him back to the City Hall.

While Gilmore was being searched in the Mayor's office, Linn took a flask of whisky from him and a fight broke out in which Gilmore cut the officer repeatedly about the face, head and hands with a razor. Linn fired four shots; two struck Gilmore, in the cheek and the right breast, and one struck Joseph Bayless, a driver who had come to help the officer and had himself been cut and kicked. Gilmore broke away toward his home and was taken without resistance by Officer Ed. Wright near the Presbyterian Church, while Linn and Bayless were carried into Ong's drug store.

Word spread that Linn had been killed, and a crowd the Intelligencer called 'vast' gathered around the Mayor's office, where there was talk of taking Gilmore and hanging him. According to the Register, 'a strong guard' was placed about the jail, and 'for a time an appeal to Judge Lynch was imminent'. The Belmont Chronicle wrote that the crowd spoke freely of 'a rope and a lamp-post'. When it was learned that Bayless would recover and Linn had a chance, the crowd cooled and, in the Register's words, decided to let the law take its course.

By the next day the Register reported that the talk of lynching had 'almost entirely abated', though remarks that Gilmore ought to be hanged could still be heard. All three wounded men recovered; Gilmore was reported almost healed in the county jail in September. No arrests of anyone in the crowd are reported.

After a preliminary hearing before Mayor Mitchell on July 31, Gilmore was held in $1,000 bail and taken to the county jail at St. Clairsville on August 1. A grand jury indicted him in November for cutting with intent to kill, and the court assigned Lorenzo Danford to defend him. His first trial ended on December 2 with a jury reported to stand 11 to 1 for conviction, and at a second trial on December 18 he was found guilty of the lesser charge of cutting with intent to wound. Judge St. Clair Kelly sentenced him on December 26 to four years in the penitentiary, and Sheriff Hilles took him to Columbus two days later.

The two Wheeling dailies, across the river, covered the affair in detail the next morning, the Intelligencer under 'A Regular Texas Time' and the Register under 'The Deadly Razor'. The Register called Gilmore 'demoniac' and a 'colored fiend', and the following day wrote that lynching would be 'unnecessary' because the officer's shot would end his life.

The Register's text went out as a Wheeling dispatch to the Philadelphia Press and appeared in the Savannah Morning News as 'A Deadly Duel in Ohio', with a closing line that 'the mob dispersed'. A shortened version in the Woodsfield Spirit of Democracy, headed 'Two Men Fatally Carved by a Negro', left out the crowd altogether. The county-seat Belmont Chronicle wrote that had the two men died 'we would most likely have had a lynching to record', since both were 'good and well-known citizens'.

Accounts differ on who struck first: the Register and the wire copy said Linn clubbed Gilmore with his mace before the razor came out, while the Intelligencer had Gilmore attacking as the flask was taken. The Belmont Chronicle wrote that the officer reached for his mace but was cut before he could draw it, and Gilmore himself told reporters he had acted in self-defense after Linn struck him with the mace.

accounts.label: Wheeling Register (and wire version)
accounts.gist: Gilmore grew 'abusive and insulting' during the search; Lynn drew his mace and clubbed him, and at the first blow Gilmore drew a razor.

accounts.label: Wheeling Intelligencer
accounts.gist: Gilmore began the razor assault while the officer was taking his whisky flask from him.

accounts.label: Belmont Chronicle
accounts.gist: Gilmore objected to the flask being taken; the officer reached for his mace but Gilmore cut him before he could draw it.

accounts.label: Gilmore's statement
accounts.gist: He bore Linn no malice and used his razor in self-defense after Linn assaulted him with his mace; he 'was not going to be imposed upon'.

framing.detail: The Register's 'The Deadly Razor' called Gilmore 'demoniac' and a 'colored fiend' and the next day remarked that lynching would be 'unnecessary' because Lynn's shot would kill him, while also reporting that the officer struck first.
The Intelligencer's 'A Regular Texas Time' gave the fullest account, including Gilmore's own version, and reported the lynching talk without comment.
The Belmont Chronicle said a lynching would 'most likely' have followed had the two 'good and well-known citizens' died.
The Savannah Morning News ran the Philadelphia Press dispatch as 'A Deadly Duel in Ohio'; the Woodsfield Spirit of Democracy ran a shorter version as 'Two Men Fatally Carved by a Negro'.

conflicts.note: The Register's and Gilmore's versions agree that the mace came first; no testimony from the trials appears in the coverage.
Local papers and the court reports consistently print Otho.
McLain appears once, in a St. Clairsville letter; Linn and Lynn are spelling variants.
The local Register's 'Exley' is the likeliest reading.
